title: The pigeonhole principle
objectives: Force a coincidence by counting boxes and objects.

screens.title: Socks in the dark
screens.prose: A drawer holds 7 red, 9 blue and 4 green socks, and the light is off. Play the unluckiest drawer. Drag socks into your hand one at a time, dodging a pair as long as you can.

state.caption: Drag socks from the drawer into your hand.

screens.question: Stop at the first sock that must make a pair of one colour. Leave that many in your hand.

hints.text: How many socks can you hold with no two of one colour?
One red, one blue and one green: three socks, no pair.
The next sock matches one of those three, whatever its colour. So 4.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Build the unluckiest hand first, then add one.

byKey.count-hand: Count again: the unluckiest hand holds one sock of each colour, and the next one makes a pair.

explain.text: The worst case is one sock of each colour: three socks and no pair. The fourth sock must match one of them, so 4 is enough and 3 is not. Principle: for 'how many to be sure', build the worst case, then add one.

screens.title: Two that sum to 13
screens.prose: You pick numbers from 1 to 12, as unluckily as you like.
screens.question: How many must you pick to be sure that two of them sum to 13?

canvas.caption: 1 to 6: six numbers, and no two sum to 13.

hints.text: Which pairs sum to 13? Treat each pair as a box.
1 with 12, 2 with 11, and so on: six pairs.
Six boxes. Seven numbers put two in one box.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Pair the numbers that sum to 13 and count the pairs.

byKey.six: Six can fail: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6 contain no pair summing to 13.
byKey.two: Two numbers sum to 13 only when you choose well. Here the picks are unlucky.
byKey.thirteen: There are only 12 numbers. Pair them up first.

explain.text: The pairs (1, 12), (2, 11), ..., (6, 7) are six boxes, so seven numbers put two in one box. Six can fail: 1 to 6 has no such pair. Principle: name the boxes and count them.

canvas.caption: Six pairs that sum to 13: the boxes.

screens.title: Handshakes at a party
screens.prose: Six guests meet at a party, and some pairs shake hands once. Nobody shakes their own hand.

state.caption: One possible party. The number under each guest counts their handshakes.

screens.question: Must two guests have shaken the same number of hands?

options.text: No: the counts 0 to 5 give six different values
options.why: You used all six counts, but 0 and 5 cannot both occur.

options.text: Only if someone shook no hands
options.why: Even with everyone shaking hands, the counts run 1 to 5: five values for six guests.

hints.text: What counts can a guest have?
From 0 to 5. Can a 0 and a 5 both happen?
A guest with 5 shook everyone's hand, so nobody has 0. Five values, six guests.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask whether 0 and 5 can occur at the same party.

byKey.no: A 5 means everyone shook that guest's hand, so nobody has 0.
byKey.some: With no 0, the counts run 1 to 5: still five values for six guests.

explain.text: Counts run from 0 to 5, but 0 and 5 cannot both occur: a 5 shook everyone's hand. So six guests fall into five boxes, and two share a count. Principle: when the boxes outnumber the objects, look for boxes that cannot both be used.

screens.title: Prove the handshake fact
screens.prose: Put the proof in order. Two lines may swap, and one line does not belong.

state.caption: One possible party. The number under each guest counts their handshakes.

screens.question: Order the proof that two guests share a count.

lines.text: Each guest shook between 0 and 5 hands: six possible counts.
If someone shook 5 hands, everyone shook at least one, so 0 is missing.
If someone shook 0 hands, nobody shook 5.
So at most five counts occur among the six guests.
By the pigeonhole principle, two guests share a count.
Everyone shakes at least one hand, so the counts run from 1 to 5.
lines.why: Nothing forces a guest to shake hands. The proof must handle a guest with 0.

hints.text: Start with the range of possible counts.
Then show that 0 and 5 cannot both appear.
Range, the two cases, five counts at most, pigeonhole.

feedback.correct: Range, two cases, five counts, pigeonhole.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Rule out 0 and 5 together before you count.

byKey.d1: That line assumes everyone shakes hands. A guest may shake none.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the one assuming everyone shakes hands belongs.

explain.text: The two cases rule out 0 and 5 together, which leaves five boxes for six guests. The pigeonhole principle then forces a shared count. Principle: show some boxes cannot all be used.

screens.title: Two blue socks
screens.prose: Back to the drawer: 7 red, 9 blue and 4 green socks in the dark. A candidate answers at once with 4, the answer for a pair.

state.caption: 7 red, 9 blue and 4 green socks, drawn in the dark.

screens.question: How many socks must you take to be sure of two blue ones?

hints.text: Who decides which socks come out? Assume the worst.
The worst case takes every red and every green first.
$7 + 4 = 11$ socks with no blue, then 2 blue.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take every non-blue sock first, then two blues.

byKey.pair: That is the answer for any pair. Two blues ask for a different worst case.
byKey.three: You allowed one sock per colour. The unlucky draw can take all 11 red and green socks first.
byKey.eleven: Eleven socks may all be red and green. You still need two blue.
byKey.two: Two socks could both be red.

explain.text: The worst case takes all 7 red and all 4 green socks: 11 socks and no blue. Two more must both be blue, so 13. Principle: the worst case depends on the question, so rebuild it each time.

screens.title: The pigeonhole principle
screens.prose: Each time you named boxes and objects. With more objects than boxes, two share a box. $$n \text{ objects in } k \text{ boxes} \implies \text{some box holds at least } \lceil n/k \rceil.$$ For 'how many to be sure', build the worst case, then add one. You met the idea in Reasoning and Proof, lesson 9, and Counting and Chance, lesson 10 (the birthday problem).
screens.question: In the sum-13 puzzle, what were the boxes?

options.why: The numbers are the objects you pick. Twelve boxes would need 13 picks.
Sums are not what you place. Each pick lands in its pair.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The boxes are what a pick lands in.

byKey.numbers: The numbers are the objects, not the boxes.
byKey.sums: Each pick lands in a pair, not a sum.

explain.text: Each number lands in its pair, so six pairs are six boxes. Seven picks put two numbers in one pair, and those two sum to 13. Choosing the boxes is the whole art.

screens.question: Must two of any ten points in the square be within $\sqrt{2} \approx 1.414$ of each other?

options.text: No: space them on a grid 1.5 apart
options.why: That grid holds nine points. A tenth must share a unit square with one of them.

options.text: Only if the points sit on whole numbers
options.why: Where they sit does not matter. Cut the square into nine unit squares.

hints.text: Cut the square into nine unit squares.
Ten points, nine squares: two share one.
Two points in one unit square are at most its diagonal apart, $\sqrt{2}$.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Use nine unit squares as boxes.

byKey.grid: Nine points fit 1.5 apart, but the tenth lands in a unit square with another.
byKey.whole: Position does not matter: nine boxes, ten points.

explain.text: Nine unit squares hold ten points, so two share a square, at most $\sqrt{2}$ apart. Nine points 1.5 apart show nine are not enough. Principle: in geometry, the boxes are regions of small diameter.

screens.title: Drill: trades and counterparties
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes. A desk books 40 trades with 13 counterparties.
screens.question: What is the largest number you can be sure some counterparty traded at least?

hints.text: Spread the trades as evenly as possible.
Three trades each covers $3 \times 13 = 39$.
The 40th trade gives some counterparty a fourth.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how many trades 13 counterparties can take at three each.

byKey.three: Three each covers only 39 trades. The 40th makes a fourth.
byKey.thirteen: You gave the number of counterparties. Divide the trades among them.

explain.text: Three trades each covers $3 \times 13 = 39$ trades, so the 40th forces a fourth. Spreading 40 as one 4 and twelve 3s shows 5 is not certain. Principle: $n$ objects in $k$ boxes put $\lceil n/k \rceil$ in some box.

screens.title: Drill: sums and differences
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes. You pick whole numbers, as unluckily as you like.
screens.question: How many must you pick to be sure two of them have a sum or a difference divisible by 10?

hints.text: Only the remainders on division by 10 matter.
Two numbers work if their remainders are equal or add to 10.

feedback.correct: Seven numbers. Principle: merge boxes until any two in a box work.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Group the remainders so that two in one group always work.

byKey.six: Six can fail: 0, 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 have no such pair.
byKey.eleven: You used ten remainders as boxes. Remainders 1 and 9 can share a box, since their sum is 10.
byKey.ten: Ten is the number of remainders, not of picks. Merged pairs leave six boxes, so seven picks.

explain.text: Group the remainders as {0}, {5}, {1, 9}, {2, 8}, {3, 7} and {4, 6}. Two numbers in one group have a sum or difference divisible by 10. Six boxes force it at seven, and 0 to 5 shows six can fail.

screens.title: Drill: two of every colour
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes. The drawer again: 7 red, 9 blue and 4 green socks in the dark.

state.caption: 7 red, 9 blue and 4 green socks, drawn in the dark.

screens.question: How many socks must you take to be sure of two of every colour?

hints.text: Which colour can the unlucky draw hold back longest?
Green is the smallest pile, so it can come out last.
All 9 blue and all 7 red first: 16 socks, then 2 green.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Let the draw empty the two biggest piles before any green.

byKey.six: Two of each only happens if the draw is kind. The worst case is far longer.
byKey.thirteen: That makes two blue certain, not two of every colour.
byKey.seventeen: After 16 non-green socks, one green is not two.
byKey.twenty: You took every sock. After 18, two of each colour are already certain.

explain.text: The worst case empties the blue and red piles first, 16 socks, and holds back green. Two more are both green, so 18. Principle: the worst case for 'every colour' starves the smallest pile.

screens.title: Three of one colour
screens.prose: Follow-up. The interviewer swaps the drawer for one with four colours and plenty of each. Now they want three socks of one colour.
screens.question: How many must you take to be sure?

hints.text: Build the worst case: as many socks as possible with no three alike.
Two of each colour: 8 socks.
The ninth sock makes three of its colour.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Hold two of each colour, then add one.

byKey.four: Four socks give a pair at most. Three of one colour needs more.
byKey.twelve: You took three of each. Two of each, plus one, is enough.
byKey.thirteen: You took three of each and added one. Two of each is the worst case.
byKey.eight: Eight socks can be two of each colour, with no three alike.

explain.text: The worst case holds two socks of each colour: $4 \times 2 = 8$ with no three alike. The ninth makes three. Principle: the worst case fills every box to one below the target.

screens.title: The general rule
screens.prose: The interviewer generalises: $k$ colours, plenty of each, and you want $r$ socks of one colour. Hashing uses the same count: $n$ keys in $k$ buckets put at least $\lceil n/k \rceil$ in one bucket. Reasoning and Proof, lesson 9, used it for hash buckets.
screens.question: How many socks make it certain?

hints.text: Use the worst case from the last screen.
With four colours and $r = 3$ you held $4 \times 2$ socks.
Hold $r - 1$ of each of $k$ colours, then add one.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the worst case for $k$ colours, then add one.

byKey.kr: You held $r$ of each colour. That already has $r$ alike; hold $r - 1$.
byKey.kr0: That holds $r$ of each colour. The worst case holds $r - 1$, then adds one.

explain.text: The worst case holds $r - 1$ socks of each colour, $k(r - 1)$ in all, with no $r$ alike. One more forces $r$ of a colour. Principle: fill every box to one below the target, then add one.

ideas: Name the boxes and the objects: more objects than boxes puts two in one box.
With $n$ objects in $k$ boxes, some box holds at least $\lceil n/k \rceil$.
For 'how many to be sure', build the worst case, then add one.
summary.trap: Two blue socks need 13, not 4: the worst case takes every other sock first.

quiz.question: Can six numbers avoid any pair that sums to 13?

options.text: No: six numbers always contain such a pair
options.why: Seven force a pair. Six can take one number from each of the six pairs.

options.text: Yes, but only the set 1 to 6
options.why: Any one number from each pair works, such as 12, 11, 10, 4, 5 and 6.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take one number from each pair.

byKey.no: Take one number from each pair, such as 1 to 6: no two sum to 13.
byKey.only: Any one number from each pair works, such as 12, 11, 10, 4, 5 and 6.

explain.text: One number from each of the six pairs, such as 1 to 6, has no pair summing to 13. So 6 is not enough and 7 is needed. Principle: the bound is tight when one object per box is possible.

quiz.prose: A box holds 100 chocolates in 4 flavours.
quiz.question: What is the largest number you can be sure some flavour reaches?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide 100 among 4 flavours as evenly as you can.

byKey.twentysix: Twenty-five of each fills the box exactly, so 26 is not certain.
byKey.twentyfour: Twenty-four of each makes only 96, so some flavour has at least 25.

explain.text: Twenty-four of each flavour makes only 96, so some flavour has at least 25. Twenty-five of each shows 26 is not certain. Principle: $\lceil n/k \rceil$ is the guarantee.

quiz.prose: People walk into a room one by one.
quiz.question: How many must be in the room to be sure two share a birth month?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Twelve months are twelve boxes.

byKey.twelve: Twelve people can all have different months.
byKey.twentyfive: That forces three in one month. Two needs only 13.

explain.text: Twelve months are twelve boxes, and twelve people can fill one each. The thirteenth must share. Principle: one more object than boxes forces a shared box.
